name: FUNW(history)
prose: int FUNW(history)(TYPE(History) *h, TYPE(HistEvent) *ev, int fun, ...) (libedit history.c lines 997-1167; the wide/narrow name is selected by the FUNW macro; slice cut head). Precondition: h and ev are valid, and the variadic arguments match what the command fun expects. Postcondition: it first sets ev's error state to _HE_OK, then dispatches on fun and returns the command's result (0 or positive on success, -1 on failure). Commands that set the error on failure: H_LOAD (_HE_HIST_READ), H_SAVE, H_SAVE_FP and H_NSAVE_FP (_HE_HIST_WRITE), H_FUNC (_HE_PARAM_MISSING when history_set_fun fails) and an unknown fun (-1 with _HE_UNKNOWN); the other commands delegate to the history_* helpers or to the backend functions, which set the error themselves. H_ENTER stores ev->num in h->h_ent only when the enter succeeds; H_APPEND does HSET(h_ent) and then HADD only if that succeeded; H_CLEAR returns 0; H_FUNC sets h->h_ent to -1 before building the new backend table and keeps that value even if history_set_fun then fails; H_END calls the history end function and returns 0. H_REPLACE (documented as only valid after H_NEXT_EVDATA) dereferences the default history's cursor and returns -1 without setting an error if line is NULL or Strdup fails; otherwise it replaces the cursor's string and data pointers and returns 0. H_DELDATA and H_NEXT_EVDATA call the default-history helpers directly.
note: reviewers RIGHT: R1 (H_REPLACE failure does not set ev's error) and R15 (H_REPLACE needs a prior H_NEXT_EVDATA; H_FUNC sets h_ent = -1 even if it fails)

name: history_set_fun
prose: static int history_set_fun(TYPE(History) *h, TYPE(History) *nh) (libedit history.c lines 723-764; slice cut head). Precondition: h and nh point to History objects. Postcondition: if any of nh->h_first, nh->h_next, nh->h_last, nh->h_prev, nh->h_curr, nh->h_set, nh->h_enter, nh->h_add, nh->h_clear, nh->h_del or nh->h_ref is NULL it returns -1; before returning, if h is not using the default backend (h->h_next != history_def_next) it calls history_def_init to create a fresh default history in h->h_ref (the previous h_ref is not freed here) and, only if that succeeds, resets the function table to the default functions; if history_def_init fails it returns -1 and leaves h unchanged; if h already uses the default backend nothing is changed. When all of nh's fields are non-NULL: if h uses the default backend its entries are cleared with history_def_clear (the history_t structure itself stays), then h->h_ent is set to -1 and the ten function pointers (h_first, h_next, h_last, h_prev, h_curr, h_set, h_clear, h_enter, h_add, h_del) are copied from nh and 0 is returned. h->h_ref itself is not assigned from nh in this function.
note: reviewers RIGHT: R1 (history_def_init failure leaves h unchanged) and R15 (the NULL check is on nh->h_next, not h->h_next); also noted h_ref is not copied

name: read__fixio
prose: static int read__fixio(int fd, int e) (libedit read.c lines 147-202). The fd parameter is marked __attribute__((unused)) but is used by the recovery calls. Precondition: fd is an open descriptor; e is the errno from a failed read, or -1. Postcondition: for e == EINTR it returns 0. For e == -1, EWOULDBLOCK (when defined), or EAGAIN (only when POSIX is defined and EAGAIN differs from EWOULDBLOCK) it sets a result of 0 and, if a recovery is compiled in, tries: with F_SETFL and O_NDELAY, fcntl(fd, F_GETFL) followed by fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, flags & ~O_NDELAY), and, with FIONBIO, ioctl(fd, FIONBIO, &0); a failure of any of these calls returns -1 at once; if at least one succeeded it returns 0, and if none is compiled in (or the case is not reached via TRY_AGAIN) it returns -1. Any other e returns -1. So it can clear the non-blocking mode of fd, and it modifies nothing else.
note: reviewer RIGHT (R15): fd is used by fcntl/ioctl; R2 (EAGAIN only handled when distinct from EWOULDBLOCK) RIGHT

name: re_update_line
prose: static void re_update_line(EditLine *el, wchar_t *old, wchar_t *new, int i) (libedit refresh.c lines 540-1004; slice shows part of it). Precondition: old and new are writable NUL-terminated wide strings holding the displayed and wanted contents of screen line i. Postcondition: it finds the first differing position, finds the ends of both strings, strips trailing blanks from the end of old and of new by writing a NUL there (so both buffers can be modified), and returns at once if no difference remains. Otherwise it finds the last common part, looks for an insertion or deletion alignment (case 1 and case 2), applies tuning for a terminal that cannot insert or delete (EL_CAN_INSERT/EL_CAN_DELETE) and a minimum run of 4 characters worth keeping, computes the net insert/delete counts fx (first difference) and sx (second difference), and moves the cursor to line i. It then, in order: does a first-difference insert (when fx > 0, the inserted text fits on the line width, and the first difference lies before the kept text), or a first-difference delete (when fx < 0), overwriting with new text and updating old with re__strncopy/re_insert/re_delete; each of these two returns from the function when there is nothing to keep at the end of the line (the delete case clears to end of line first); then a second-difference delete (sx < 0), a late first-difference insert (when it was not done early), and a second-difference insert or overwrite (sx >= 0). It returns nothing; terminal output goes through terminal_* calls, and only the first-difference steps copy text into old.
note: reviewer WRONG (R17): the code does write NUL at oe and ne (lines 572, 584) and so modifies new; slice cut head, real name re_update_line (line 541); read the whole function

name: terminal_echotc
prose: libedit_private int terminal_echotc(EditLine *el, int argc, const wchar_t **argv) (terminal.c lines 1450-1664; slice shows lines 1566-1664). Precondition: argv is NULL or a NULL-terminated vector: argv[0] the command name, then an optional -v or -s (other '-x' flags are skipped silently), then a capability name and its arguments. Postcondition: returns -1 if argv is NULL or has no word after the command name. With no capability word (or an empty one) it returns 0. The special names tabs, meta, xn, am, baud, rows/lines and cols print their value to el_outfile and return 0. Otherwise the capability string comes from the local table or tgetstr; if it is missing or empty a diagnostic is printed to el_errfile (unless -s) and -1 is returned. The number of parameters arg_need is counted from the % escapes of the string (unknown escapes print a warning only with -v). arg_need 0: an extra argument gives a warning (unless -s) and -1, otherwise the string is output through terminal_tputs and 0 is returned. arg_need 1: one non-negative integer argument (used as the row, column 0) is required: missing, malformed or negative gives a message (unless -s) and -1, an extra argument gives -1, otherwise terminal_tputs(tgoto(...), 1) and 0. arg_need 2: two non-negative integer arguments (cols then rows) are required with the same -1 failures, then terminal_tputs(tgoto(scap, cols, rows), rows) and 0. arg_need greater than 2 prints 'Too many required arguments' to el_errfile when -v is given (not suppressed by -s) and then continues exactly like the two-argument case, so such a capability returns -1 only if the two arguments are bad or extra arguments exist.
note: reviewers: R15 (-s does not suppress the verbose 'Too many required arguments' warning) RIGHT; R17 (arg_need > 2 warns and parses two args, returning 0 on success) RIGHT; slice cut head

name: FUN(tok,line)
prose: Generated function tok_line(tok, line, argc, argv, cursorc, cursoro), named FUN(tok,line) in the source (tokenizer.c lines 205-450; wide-character variant tok_wline). Precondition: tok comes from tok_init and is not destroyed, line describes the text (buffer, cursor, lastchar), argc and argv are non-NULL, cursorc and cursoro may be NULL. Postcondition: it walks the text one character at a time, building words in the tokenizer's own buffer with Bourne-shell style quoting (single quotes, double quotes, backslash escapes). It returns 0 when it reaches an unquoted newline or the end of the text in the unquoted state with no pending line-continuation: the current word is finished, *argv and *argc are set to the tokenizer's vector and word count, and if cursorc/cursoro are non-NULL they receive the word index and the offset within the word of the cursor; when the cursor position was not reached before the end (for example the cursor is at lastchar) they receive the index and length of the position after the last word, not -1. It returns 1 if the text ends inside single quotes, 2 if it ends inside double quotes, and 3 if the text ends in the unquoted state while a backslash-newline continuation is pending (TOK_EAT set by a backslash followed by newline); it returns -1 for an invalid quote state or when growing the word buffer or the argument vector fails. A newline inside single or double quotes is kept in the word. A trailing backslash at the end of the text stores a NUL byte and does not return by itself. On a nonzero return *argc and *argv are not set and the tokenizer state is partial, to be cleared with tok_reset. The returned vector and words belong to tok.
note: reviewer RIGHT (R15): 3 is for a pending line continuation (backslash-newline) at the end, not a newline inside quotes; also the old claim of -1 cursor values is wrong: tok_line_outok fills them with the end position (lines 438-441)

name: FUN(tok,str)
prose: Generated function tok_str(tok, line, argc, argv), named FUN(tok,str) in the source (tokenizer.c lines 456-466; wide variant tok_wstr). Precondition: tok is an initialised Tokenizer, line is a NUL-terminated string, argc and argv are non-NULL. Postcondition: it builds a LineInfo with buffer = line and cursor = lastchar = the end of the string and calls tok_line without cursor outputs, returning that result: 0 with *argc set to the word count and *argv set to the tokenizer's word vector, both when the whole string is consumed and also when an unquoted newline ends the parse before the end of the string (the rest of the string is ignored); 1 for an unterminated single quote at the end, 2 for an unterminated double quote, 3 when a backslash-newline continuation is pending at the end, and -1 for an invalid quote state or an allocation failure while growing the buffers. On any nonzero return *argc and *argv are not assigned and the tokenizer state may have been modified.
note: reviewer RIGHT (R15): a newline in the unquoted state returns 0 before the end of the string

name: vi_to_next_char
prose: libedit_private el_action_t vi_to_next_char(EditLine *el, wint_t c) (vi.c lines 753-758, the vi 't' command; c is unused). Postcondition: returns cv_csearch(el, CHAR_FWD, -1, el->el_state.argument, 1): it reads the next character from the input (end of file -> ed_end_of_file), records the search (character, direction, till-flag 1) for ';' and ',', and searches forward from the cursor, count times, for that character; the final tflag of 1 means 'till': the cursor stops one character before the matching character, not on it. If a vi operator is pending the region up to the match is deleted/yanked through cv_delfini and CC_REFRESH is returned; otherwise it returns CC_CURSOR. If the character is not found before the end of the line it returns CC_ERROR.
note: reviewers RIGHT: the last argument 1 is the till flag (cv_csearch, search.c:599-644), so the cursor stops before the match

name: vi_to_prev_char
prose: libedit_private el_action_t vi_to_prev_char(EditLine *el, wint_t c) (vi.c lines 765-770, the vi 'T' command; c is unused). Postcondition: returns cv_csearch(el, CHAR_BACK, -1, el->el_state.argument, 1): it reads the next character, records the search for ';' and ',', and searches backward from the cursor, count times; with the till flag the cursor stops one character after the matching character (cp -= direction), not on it. With a pending vi operator the region is deleted or yanked through cv_delfini and CC_REFRESH is returned; otherwise CC_CURSOR is returned. If the character is not found before the start of the line it returns CC_ERROR.
note: reviewers RIGHT: tflag 1 makes the cursor stop after the match when searching backward

name: evbuffer_read
prose: int evbuffer_read(struct evbuffer *buf, evutil_socket_t fd, int howmuch) (libevent buffer.c lines 2283-2412; slice cut head). Precondition: buf is a valid evbuffer whose lock the caller does not hold; fd is a readable descriptor. Postcondition: it takes the buffer lock and releases it before returning. It returns -1 without reading if buf->freeze_end is set. Otherwise the amount to read is the number of readable bytes reported by FIONREAD (EVBUFFER_MAX_READ if that is unavailable, not positive or too large), and howmuch below 0 or above that amount is replaced by it. It makes room with evbuffer_expand_fast_ (or evbuffer_expand_singlechain) and returns -1 if that fails. The expansion can already have added capacity or chains to the buffer even if the following read fails or reports EOF. It then reads with readv (or read, or WSARecv/recv). A result of -1 (on Windows also a WSARecv error other than WSAECONNABORTED) returns -1; a result of 0 (including WSAECONNABORTED) returns 0; in both cases no data has been added. For n > 0 it advances the chains' off fields (and last_with_datap), adds n to buf->total_len and n_add_for_cb, invokes the buffer callbacks and returns n.
note: reviewer RIGHT (R15): the read-failure and EOF returns leave the data unchanged but the expansion step may already have changed the buffer capacity

name: do_read
prose: static int do_read(struct bufferevent_openssl *bev_ssl, int n_to_read) (bufferevent_openssl.c lines 583-649). Precondition: the caller holds the bufferevent lock. Postcondition: returns a bitmask of OP_MADE_PROGRESS (1), OP_BLOCKED (2) and OP_ERR (4). It returns 0 at once when reading is suspended. It limits n_to_read by the read rate limit and reserves input space with evbuffer_reserve_space (up to 2 vectors); if that fails it returns OP_ERR alone (no conn_closed call). For each reserved vector (stopping if reading becomes suspended) it calls SSL_read: on success it adds OP_MADE_PROGRESS, clears read-blocked-on-write if it was set (a clear_rbow failure returns OP_ERR | result at once, before the pending reads are committed), counts the vector and decrements the rate-limit buckets; on failure it examines SSL_get_error: WANT_READ clears read-blocked-on-write if it was set, WANT_WRITE sets it if it was not set (in both cases a failure of clear_rbow/set_rbow returns OP_ERR | result, which can be OP_ERR alone when nothing was read yet); any other error calls conn_closed with BEV_EVENT_READING; after any of these OP_BLOCKED is added and the loop stops. Finally, if n vectors were filled, it commits them to the input buffer (not done on the OP_ERR early returns) and, if there is an underlying bufferevent, resets the generic read timeout, and returns the result mask.
note: reviewers RIGHT: R1 (OP_ERR paths skip conn_closed; clear_rbow failure after progress skips the commit) and R15 (OP_ERR alone can also come from clear_rbow/set_rbow failing with no progress)

name: do_write
prose: static int do_write(struct bufferevent_openssl *bev_ssl, int atmost) (bufferevent_openssl.c lines 653-730). Precondition: the caller holds the bufferevent lock. The atmost parameter is overwritten before being used: it becomes last_write when that is positive, otherwise the write rate limit. Postcondition: returns a bitmask of OP_MADE_PROGRESS (1), OP_BLOCKED (2) and OP_ERR (4). If evbuffer_peek on the output fails it returns OP_ERR alone (no conn_closed call). For each peeked vector (stopping if writing becomes suspended, skipping empty vectors) it calls SSL_write: on success it adds OP_MADE_PROGRESS, clears write-blocked-on-read if it was set (a clear_wbor failure returns OP_ERR | result at once, without draining the bytes already written in this call, resetting the write timeout or triggering EV_WRITE), adds r to n_written, sets last_write to -1 and decrements the rate-limit buckets; on failure it examines SSL_get_error: WANT_WRITE clears write-blocked-on-read if set and records the vector length in last_write, WANT_READ sets write-blocked-on-read if not set (a set_wbor failure returns OP_ERR | result, which can be OP_ERR alone) and records last_write, any other error calls conn_closed with BEV_EVENT_WRITING and sets last_write to -1; after these OP_BLOCKED is added and the loop stops. Finally, if n_written is non-zero it drains that many bytes from the output buffer, resets the generic write timeout if an underlying bufferevent exists, and triggers a deferred EV_WRITE callback; it returns the result mask.
note: reviewers RIGHT: R1 (clear_wbor failure after progress returns OP_ERR|OP_MADE_PROGRESS without draining) and R15 (OP_ERR alone can also come from clear_wbor/set_wbor failing with no progress); atmost parameter ignored

name: event_add_nolock_
prose: int event_add_nolock_(struct event *ev, const struct timeval *tv, int tv_is_absolute) (libevent event.c lines 2596-2766; slice cut head). Precondition: the caller holds ev->ev_base's base lock, ev has been set up with an event base, and tv, when non-NULL, is a valid timeval. Postcondition: returns -1 at once if the event is finalizing (EVLIST_FINALIZING), or if tv is non-NULL, the event is not already in the timeout heap, and reserving space in the heap fails; in these cases nothing is changed. If another thread's signal callback for this event is running it first waits on the base's condition variable (which releases the lock while waiting). If the event has EV_READ/EV_WRITE/EV_CLOSED/EV_SIGNAL and is not already inserted, active or active-later it adds it to the I/O or signal map (a failure makes the function return -1 without touching the timeout; a result of 1 means the main thread must be notified) and marks it inserted. If tv is non-NULL and no failure occurred, it records a persistent event's timeout interval, removes the event from the timeout queue and from the active queue if it was active because of a timeout, and sets ev_timeout to tv itself when tv_is_absolute, otherwise to the current time plus tv; for a common timeout the microsecond field of tv is masked when added to the current time and the common-timeout index bits of tv_usec are copied into ev_timeout. It then inserts the event in the timeout structure and, for a common timeout, reschedules the list if the event is first; otherwise, if the event became the earliest heap element (or the top element's timeout is already in the past), it flags a notification. With a notification pending and the base needing notification, evthread_notify_base is called. Returns 0 on success, including the case where tv is NULL and nothing needed adding; the lock is held on return.
note: reviewers RIGHT: R1 (0 returned with no insertion when tv is NULL and no I/O/signal flags) and R15 (common timeouts keep the index bits and mask the microseconds, lines 2717-2722); the lock can be released temporarily by EVTHREAD_COND_WAIT

name: event_reinit
prose: int event_reinit(struct event_base *base) (libevent event.c lines 980-1086; slice cut head). Precondition: base is a valid event base, normally just after fork. Postcondition: it takes the base lock for the whole call. If the backend needs reinit, it temporarily replaces base->evsel with nil_eventop so that deleting the internal events does not touch the shared backend. If the signal-notification event was added (ev_signal_added) it is deleted, unassigned, zeroed and remembered; the two ev_signal_pair descriptors are closed when they are not -1 (these deletions happen regardless of need_reinit). If a thread-notification function exists it is cleared and was_notifiable is remembered; if th_notify_fd[0] is not -1 the th_notify event is deleted, its descriptors closed and set to -1. The original evsel is restored. If the backend needs reinit: its dealloc (if any) is called and evsel->init is called again (a NULL result calls event_errx(1, ...), which does not return in the default configuration; if it did, res = -1), the changelist memory is freed and evmap_reinit_ is called (failure sets res = -1); in that branch the signal event is not re-added by this function itself (evmap_reinit_, which I did not read, re-informs the backend of pending events). Otherwise it calls evsig_init_ and, when it succeeds and the signal event had been added, re-adds it with event_add_nolock_ (setting ev_signal_added on success). If the base was notifiable and nothing failed it calls evthread_make_base_notifiable_nolock_. It releases the lock and returns res: 0 on success or -1 if evmap_reinit_, evsig_init_, event_add_nolock_ or evthread_make_base_notifiable_nolock_ failed.
note: reviewer R1 RIGHT (internal events deleted regardless of need_reinit); R15 (signal event re-added in both branches) MIXED: the explicit re-add is only in the else branch (lines 1070-1075); evmap_reinit_ was not read

name: name##_HT_INIT
prose: Macro-generated function name##_HT_INIT(struct name *head) defined inside HT_PROTOTYPE(name, type, field, hashfn, eqfn) in libevent ht-internal.h (the real name is name##_HT_INIT for the chosen hash-table name). Precondition: head points to a writable hash-table head. Postcondition: sets hth_table to NULL and hth_table_length, hth_n_entries and hth_load_limit to 0 and hth_prime_idx to -1; any previous table is not freed. Returns nothing.

name: name##_HT_FIND_P_
prose: Macro-generated function name##_HT_FIND_P_(struct name *head, struct type *elm) defined inside HT_PROTOTYPE(name, type, field, hashfn, eqfn) in libevent ht-internal.h (the real name is name##_HT_FIND_P_ for the chosen hash-table name). Precondition: head and elm are valid; when hash values are cached elm's hash must already be set; if the table pointer is non-NULL its length is non-zero. Postcondition: returns NULL if head->hth_table is NULL; otherwise returns the address of the link in elm's bucket chain that points to the first element for which eqfn(*p, elm) is true, or the address of the chain's terminating NULL link if there is no match. The table is not modified.

name: name##_HT_FIND
prose: Macro-generated function name##_HT_FIND(const struct name *head, struct type *elm) defined inside HT_PROTOTYPE(name, type, field, hashfn, eqfn) in libevent ht-internal.h (the real name is name##_HT_FIND for the chosen hash-table name). Precondition: head and elm are valid. Postcondition: when hash values are cached it stores elm's hash into elm (so elm is modified despite the const head), calls name##_HT_FIND_P_ and returns the matching element, or NULL if the table has no table array or no element matches. The table is not modified.

name: name##_HT_INSERT
prose: Macro-generated function name##_HT_INSERT(struct name *head, struct type *elm) defined inside HT_PROTOTYPE(name, type, field, hashfn, eqfn) in libevent ht-internal.h (the real name is name##_HT_INSERT for the chosen hash-table name). Precondition: head and elm are valid and the table does not already contain an element matching elm. Postcondition: if the table array is absent or the entry count has reached the load limit it calls name##_HT_GROW(head, n + 1) and ignores the result (if growth fails on an absent table the bucket computation would divide by a zero length); it then increments hth_n_entries, sets elm's hash when hashes are cached, and links elm at the front of its bucket chain. Returns nothing.

name: name##_HT_REPLACE
prose: Macro-generated function name##_HT_REPLACE(struct name *head, struct type *elm) defined inside HT_PROTOTYPE(name, type, field, hashfn, eqfn) in libevent ht-internal.h (the real name is name##_HT_REPLACE for the chosen hash-table name). Precondition: head and elm are valid. Postcondition: grows the table (result ignored) if the table array is absent or at its load limit, sets elm's hash, finds the slot with FIND_P_ and stores elm there. If a different matching element r was there, elm takes over r's chain successor, r's next pointer is cleared, the count is unchanged and r is returned. Otherwise (no match, or the match is elm itself) the entry count is incremented and NULL is returned; in the no-match case elm's own next pointer is not written by this function, and if the table is still absent after a failed growth the returned slot pointer is NULL and is dereferenced.

name: name##_HT_REMOVE
prose: Macro-generated function name##_HT_REMOVE(struct name *head, struct type *elm) defined inside HT_PROTOTYPE(name, type, field, hashfn, eqfn) in libevent ht-internal.h (the real name is name##_HT_REMOVE for the chosen hash-table name). Precondition: head and elm are valid. Postcondition: sets elm's hash when cached and looks up the slot with FIND_P_; if the table array is absent or no element matches it returns NULL and changes nothing else; otherwise it unlinks the matching element from its chain, clears that element's next pointer, decrements the entry count and returns that element.

name: name##_HT_FOREACH_FN
prose: Macro-generated function name##_HT_FOREACH_FN(struct name *head, int (*fn)(struct type *, void *), void *data) defined inside HT_PROTOTYPE(name, type, field, hashfn, eqfn) in libevent ht-internal.h (the real name is name##_HT_FOREACH_FN for the chosen hash-table name). Precondition: head is valid and fn is callable. Postcondition: if the table array is absent it returns at once; otherwise it visits every element of every bucket, saving the next link before calling fn(element, data); if fn returns non-zero the element is unlinked from its chain (its own next pointer is not cleared) and the entry count is decremented, so fn may free the element it is given. Returns nothing.

name: name##_HT_START
prose: Macro-generated function name##_HT_START(struct name *head) defined inside HT_PROTOTYPE(name, type, field, hashfn, eqfn) in libevent ht-internal.h (the real name is name##_HT_START for the chosen hash-table name). Precondition: head is valid. Postcondition: returns the address of the first non-NULL bucket slot in index order, or NULL if the table array is absent or all buckets are empty; nothing is modified.

prose: Macro-generated function name##_HT_NEXT(struct name *head, struct type **elm) defined inside HT_PROTOTYPE(name, type, field, hashfn, eqfn) in libevent ht-internal.h (the real name is name##_HT_NEXT for the chosen hash-table name). name: name##_HT_NEXT_RMV
prose: Macro-generated function name##_HT_NEXT_RMV(struct name *head, struct type **elm) defined inside HT_PROTOTYPE(name, type, field, hashfn, eqfn) in libevent ht-internal.h (the real name is name##_HT_NEXT_RMV for the chosen hash-table name). Precondition: elm is the address of a link holding a live element of head and the table length is non-zero. Postcondition: the element is unlinked by setting *elm to its successor (its own next pointer is not cleared) and the entry count is decremented; returns elm if the successor is non-NULL, otherwise the address of the first non-NULL bucket slot after the element's bucket, or NULL if there is none.

name: evhttp_connection_done
prose: static void evhttp_connection_done(struct evhttp_connection *evcon) (libevent http.c lines 823-889; slice cut head). Precondition: evcon has at least one request at the head of its queue and that request's cb is non-NULL (it is called without a check). Postcondition: for an outgoing connection (EVHTTP_CON_OUTGOING) it remembers whether the request asked for the connection to be closed, removes the request from the queue, clears its evcon pointer, sets the state to EVCON_IDLE and, if close was requested, resets the connection; then if more requests are queued it connects (if not connected) or dispatches the next request, which changes the state; otherwise, if no close was requested it starts close detection (this does not change the state), and if close was requested and the connection is AUTOFREE it marks the connection for freeing. For an incoming connection it only sets the state to EVCON_WRITING and leaves the request queued. It then calls the request's callback exactly once. For an outgoing connection it afterwards frees the request with evhttp_request_free_auto, and if the connection was marked for freeing and the queue is still empty (the callback may have added a request) it frees the connection. For an incoming connection neither the request nor the connection is freed.
note: reviewers RIGHT: R1 (state may change when the next request is connected/dispatched) and R15 (start_detectclose does not change the state)

name: accepted_socket_invoke_user_cb
prose: static void accepted_socket_invoke_user_cb(struct event_callback *dcb, void *arg) (libevent listener.c lines 605-670, Windows IOCP listener; run as a deferred callback). Precondition: arg points to a live struct accepting_socket and neither the listener lock nor the socket lock is held. Postcondition: it takes the listener lock and the socket lock. If free_on_cb is set it calls free_and_unlock_accepting_socket (closing the socket if valid, releasing the socket lock and freeing it) followed by listener_decref_and_unlock and returns. Otherwise it increments the listener refcount and: if as->error is non-zero it clears it and uses the listener's error callback (which may be NULL); else it computes the remote address, detaches the accepted socket from the accepting_socket (as->s becomes invalid), updates the accept context and takes the connection callback (which may be NULL; if it is NULL the detached socket is not closed here). After releasing both locks it calls the error callback (with the saved error set as the socket error) if there is one, else the connection callback with the accepted socket and remote address if there is one. It then locks the listener again and calls listener_decref_and_unlock; if that returns true (the listener was freed) it returns, otherwise it takes the socket lock and calls start_accepting, which returns without posting a new AcceptEx if the listener is disabled, and reports a failure by scheduling the deferred callback again.
note: reviewers RIGHT: R1 (callbacks may be NULL; start_accepting skipped when the listener is freed) and R15 (start_accepting returns early when the listener is disabled)

name: main
prose: int main(int argc, char **argv) of the libevent https-client sample (https-client.c lines 214-544; slice cut head). Postcondition: it scans argv for -url, -crt, -ignore-cert, -data, -retries, -timeout and -help (unrecognised words are ignored; a missing option value or -help calls syntax() and goes to the error exit). It then requires a URL, parses it (malformed, scheme not http/https, or no host -> error), builds the request URI, polls the random generator (failure -> error), creates the SSL_CTX, loads trust roots (system store or the -crt file; failure -> error), enables peer verification with a certificate callback that also checks the host name, creates the event base, creates an SSL object, and creates either a plain socket bufferevent (http) or an OpenSSL bufferevent (https); the connection, request (with Host and Connection: close headers, and optional POST body read from -data, whose unopenable file gives syntax() and an error exit) are created, evhttp_make_request is called, and event_base_dispatch runs. Every failure above jumps to the error label, which sets the return value to 1 and falls into cleanup; success also reaches cleanup after the dispatch loop with return value 0 (a failed HTTP transfer reported by the callback does not change it). Cleanup frees evcon, the URI, the event base and the SSL context if they exist, and frees ssl only when the scheme was http (type == HTTP); for https the SSL object is never freed here, so if creating the OpenSSL bufferevent or anything before it takes ownership fails after SSL_new, ssl is leaked. The bufferevent, request and data file are not freed on the paths where evcon creation or later steps fail. It then runs the OpenSSL (old versions) and Winsock cleanup and returns ret.
note: reviewer RIGHT (R15): for https, type is set to HTTPS before bufferevent_openssl_socket_new (line 435) so a failure there leaks ssl; I read lines 214-544 fully

name: tinytest_main
prose: int tinytest_main(int c, const char **v, struct testgroup_t *groups) (libevent test/tinytest.c lines 466-566; slice cut head). Precondition: v[0..c-1] are the command-line words; groups ends with an entry whose prefix is NULL, each group's cases end with a NULL name. Postcondition: it parses v[1..]: --RUNNING-FORKED, --no-fork, --quiet, --verbose, --terse set the corresponding globals; --help and --list-tests call usage(); --timeout takes the next word as seconds (missing -> message on stderr and -1); an unknown option prints a message on stderr and returns -1; other words are test selectors passed to process_test_option (a negative result, after it prints 'No such test as X!' on stdout, returns -1). If no test was selected it enables all tests. It then runs, for every enabled case, testcase_run_one, and for a case flagged TT_RETRIABLE whose result is not OK it prints '[RETRYING name (n)]' after each failed attempt (including the last one) and tries again, for up to four runs in total (the counter goes 3, 2, 1, 0); each final result is counted as ok, skipped or bad. Afterwards it prints an empty line when verbosity is 0, then '<bad>/<total> TESTS FAILED. (<skipped> skipped)' if any failed, else, at verbosity >= 1, '<ok> tests ok. (<skipped> skipped)'. It returns 0 if no test failed and 1 otherwise.
note: reviewer RIGHT (R15): the RETRYING line is printed after every failed attempt including the final one (line 541 before the exit test at 542); up to 4 runs

name: select_dev
prose: static int select_dev(const fido_dev_info_t *devlist, size_t ndevs, fido_dev_t **dev, size_t *idx, int secs) in libfido2 examples/select.c (lines 58-180). Precondition: devlist holds ndevs entries; dev and idx are non-NULL. Postcondition: sets *dev = NULL and *idx = 0 and prints the device count. It returns 0 immediately if ndevs is 0. calloc failure returns -1. It tries to open each device (open_dev prints a line per success), recording the index of the last one opened. If fewer than two devices opened it returns 0: with exactly one opened, *dev points to it (without a touch check, *idx its index); with none opened, *dev stays NULL and 0 is returned. With two or more it calls fido_dev_get_touch_begin on each opened device (failure -> return -1), reads the monotonic clock (failure -> -1), then loops: sleep 200 ms, poll each remaining device with fido_dev_get_touch_status (a failed poll closes and discards that device and continues); the first touched device becomes *dev (and *idx) and the function returns 0; otherwise after each pass it checks the elapsed time (clock failure -> -1) and, when the remaining time computed from secs is not above 50 ms, prints a timeout message and returns -1. On return, if the result is not 0 then *dev is reset to NULL and *idx to 0; in all cases every opened device other than *dev is cancelled, closed and freed and the table is freed; the selected device stays open for the caller.
note: reviewers RIGHT: R1/R15 (return 0 with *dev NULL when ndevs == 0 or none opened; single device returned untouched)
